grounded_facts: Shawn Wilder suffers a cardiac event and collapses, leading to a medical emergency.
memories.memory_text: A crushing pain hit my heart—I couldn't stay up, I pitched forward, my heartbeat racing out of control. The last thing I remember is Sage Hart rushing to me.

grounded_facts: Blair Ellison tries to warn Rowan Cavendish of danger before being shot.
memories.memory_text: I remember seeing Blair Ellison trying to warn someone before he got shot, but I wasn't sure what he meant in the moment.

grounded_facts: Wesley Hale is shot and killed by Blair Ellison after attempting to execute Rowan Cavendish.
memories.memory_text: I saw Wesley Hale go down after trying to execute Rowan Cavendish—Blair Ellison shot him just in time.

grounded_facts: A violent, multi-sided confrontation unfolds in the Riverside Hospital hallway involving Northstar Studios agents, criminals, and snipers.
memories.memory_text: I saw Adrian Carter and his men going for their rigs, and then Wesley Hale pulled a pistol from his ankle to backshoot Rowan Cavendish—I heard the shots, saw Wesley Hale's chest explode as he fell, and Blair Ellison' hand nearly torn off, all while I was collapsing forward in agony.

grounded_facts: Robin Keller moves across the floor toward the dying Noel Langley, dragging his knees through his own blood.
memories.memory_text: I saw Robin Keller crawling across the floor toward me, dragging his knees through his own blood as he tried to reach me while I was lying there, dying.

grounded_facts: Sage Hart administers emergency chest compressions to Shawn Wilder in a state of panic.
memories.memory_text: I felt Sage Hart's hands pressing hard on my chest, frantic and panicked, trying to save me.

grounded_facts: Noel Langley is propped up, sweating badly, with seizures affecting his heart.
memories.memory_text: I was propped up, sweating badly, and my heart was still seizing—I could barely move on my own.

grounded_facts: Casey Keller is disarmed, handcuffed, and has the rubber appliance removed from his face by agents.
Law enforcement secures the Riverside Hospital after a confrontation, conducting searches and assessments.
Sage Hart is patted down by agents and prescription pills are taken from him.
memories.memory_text: I saw the agents disarm and cuff Casey Keller, pull the rubber mask off his face, search Sage Hart and take his pills, and then secure the Riverside Hospital while Avery Sinclair arrived to assess the scene.

grounded_facts: Avery Sinclair confirms the death of Blair Ellison to Carson Ellison.
memories.memory_text: I was told that Blair Ellison had died, though I didn't witness it myself.

grounded_facts: Morgan Cavendish silently communicates with Avery Sinclair after examining Noel Langley.
memories.memory_text: I saw Morgan Cavendish shake his head while examining me, and then he silently conferred with Avery Sinclair, which made me think something was wrong.

grounded_facts: Avery Sinclair authorizes the immediate transport of Shawn Wilder to Las Vegas via Gulfstream jet.
memories.memory_text: I was told I'd be transported to Las Vegas right away on a Gulfstream jet, and that time was of the essence.

grounded_facts: Medical response to Noel Langley's cardiac episode in the Riverside Hospital.
memories.memory_text: I remember Morgan Cavendish and Sage Hart moving quickly around me, doing what they could in the Riverside Hospital after I collapsed—I could see them working, but I couldn't speak or help myself.

grounded_facts: Shawn Wilder suffers a mild cardiac episode with recurring arrhythmia, requiring medical intervention.
memories.memory_text: I felt my heart falter and couldn't steady it, and then Morgan Cavendish was kneeling beside me, opening his case, shaking his head like something was wrong—I knew I was in real trouble.

grounded_facts: Coordinated effort to transport Shawn Wilder from the Riverside Hospital to a waiting aircraft.
memories.memory_text: I heard Avery Sinclair say I was to be taken to the roof and flown to Las Vegas, that time was critical—I was being moved with Morgan Cavendish and Sage Hart, though I couldn't stand on my own.

grounded_facts: Carson Ellison deduces and states that Morgan Cavendish is a surgeon and that Noel Langley's heart was taken for transplant, not as a trophy.

Carson Ellison deduces and confronts Avery Sinclair with the truth that Noel Langley was killed not for symbolic reasons but so his heart could be transplanted, implicating Morgan Cavendish as a surgeon, not a hitman.
memories.memory_text: I heard Carson Ellison say Morgan Cavendish isn't a hitman but a surgeon, and that my heart was taken for a transplant, not as a trophy.

grounded_facts: Carson Ellison refuses Avery Sinclair's order to return to D.C. and declares the case not closed, asserting moral opposition to Northstar Studios's actions.
Carson Ellison refuses Avery Sinclair's order to return to D.C. and declares the case not closed.
memories.memory_text: I was there when Avery Sinclair ordered Carson Ellison to return to D.C. and declared the case closed, but Carson Ellison refused and said it wasn't over—he tossed his Northstar Studios ID and said it lacked an end.

memories.memory_text: I saw Carson Ellison take aim at Valerie Sawyer's oxygen tent and fire, causing an explosion—I remember a faint smile on my face as it happened, and then the blast.

memories.memory_text: I remember the telex sliding across the table, six figures written plain—Lorenzo saying they wanted us for Shawn Wilder, like it was some kind of honor. I said 'Bulllllshit...' 'cause my gut told me this was deeper than money.
I set my fork down and wiped my hands—time to get serious. I needed to know the time frame, 'cause we weren't doing this half-assed.

I sat there silent, just staring at Reese Bellamy after he pushed for details, letting him twist in the wind while Sawyer Langley dropped that 'Pussy' bomb—he didn't even catch it at first, kept squinting like he misheard.

Sawyer Langley looked at me like she wanted to eat me alive, saying 'Darian Wilder likes pussy'—I had to bite back the urge to flinch, just gave it back flat: 'And we like that he likes,' like it was nothing.
I saw those hookers come out all beat up, and when the clerk asked if we were sharing a room, I had to say fast—'No, we're not together'—before Sawyer Langley could make it worse.
Sawyer Langley kept going on about those women like some righteous rant, and I could feel the clerk shutting down, so I just said, 'I'm gonna need a mini-bar key too,' to shut it off.

I stashed the Glock, adjusted the the weathered jacket after Sawyer Langley complained about feedback—had to make sure it was clean. Told him we’re only hitting who’s in our way, not killing women just 'cause they’re caught up in this mess.

memories.memory_text: I remember—well, I was never supposed to exist. Born a bastard, right there in Vegas, after my mom got knocked up by some nobody hood.
She came from Kansas City, chasing some dumb dream from a Dairy Queen job, ended up on the Vegas strip—same place they started calling me 'Shawn Wilder.'
I was up on that stage, helping the magician with his act—cards, sleight of hand, the usual tricks—while Shawn Wilder sat in the back playing with a deck like it meant something more.
I remember hunched over the Magician’s bed, fingers fumbling with the deck, trying to get the flick just right under his watchful eye—he didn’t say much, but I could feel it when I messed up.
Robin Thorne fumbled the eight ball and started messing up fast. The cops got curious, began watching and writing things down. Soon, my actions brought the the small case to Valerie Sawyer.

I remember standing there with Valerie Sawyer at that casino opening, flashbulbs going off, both of us smiling like we were untouchable—him thinking I was loyal, me already counting the ways to take it all from him.
I walked out after making bail and disappeared—nobody’s seen me since, and the bond expires in eighteen hours.

I'm holed up in the Riverside Hospital at Riverside Hospital in Harborview Hospital under a fake name, and now Carson Colter’s blabbing about it on the phone like it’s nothing—Eastwood Holdings are already circling, set to meet me in twenty-four hours.

I remember the moment Avery Sinclair said my lawyers sent Robin Thorne to pull me out—they were desperate to cover their own asses with the bond, but I knew the Eastwood Holdings would never let that happen.

I walked through the wreckage of last night, stepping around the passed-out girls like they were corpses—my robe caught on one of their wigs, tugged it loose, and I saw the dirt and scars underneath. I almost gagged, just let the robe fall instead of pulling it free and exposing her completely.

I was shuffling Shawn Wilder and dropping them on the bodies like they meant nothing, trying to steady my hands—Robin Keller came in gulping Mylanta, said he got the guy's machine, and I had to ask him twice, my skin crawling with impatience.
I remember screaming at Robin Hawthorne, right in his face, because he had the nerve to tell me to calm down after we got hit for fifty grand—like this was some minor setback instead of a disaster.
I remember barking orders—get the Russian to clean the place floor to ceiling, pack us up, replace the hookers, and call Carson Colter—because this dump was compromised and reeking of failure.
I remember the weight of the silence after he said I might be dead within a day — my chest tightened, but I still said I wasn't doing the old key.

I told Sage Hart it wasn't possible for him to come, but he kept pushing, talking about coma and amputations like I didn't already know—like I needed him to scare me. Finally I gave in, said fine, come to Harborview Hospital, Robin Keller’ll meet you.

Right after hanging up, I walked to Northstar Studios, rolled that hundred, and snorted one more line—told myself it was the last bit, just to get through, just to steady—felt it burn, same as always.
I saw myself in the mirror—just for a second—and it hit me how far I've fallen, standing there while everything went to shit around me.
I saw my Hookers come out of the Lakeview School after the fight—bruised, barefoot, wigs crooked, slinging broken heels. They were loud, then got surrounded and taken away.

I was lying on that sawed-off baby grand, cards in hand, shuffling over and over while the the old key sat ready—told Carson Colter straight, if they didn’t give us no jail time in ten seconds, the deal was dead.
I told Morrey I don’t have to do shit—no more cooperation—until I get what I want, and I meant it. These Eastwood Holdings are pushing, but I’m the one taking the fall if this blows up.

I saw the Joker when I pulled that card out of the air, and something just snapped—I said 'Alright...do it.' I knew it meant giving up Robin Hawthorne, Bennett Arden, all of them. Didn’t feel real, but I said it anyway.

I was packing my suits, shoving them into the bag, trying to focus on getting out, when Robin Hawthorne asked about Carson Colter and my body locked up—I couldn’t swallow right, like the lie was stuck in my throat.
I saw the the small case poking out of my bag and panicked, yanking the bedspread over it fast—then Robin Hawthorne opened his coat and I saw the .50 Cal, and I couldn’t even look him in the eye.
I pulled the cards from my pocket and shuffled them fast—left to right, right to left—making the movements sharp, hypnotic, showing Robin Hawthorne exactly what I wanted him to see, nothing more.
I said the Eastwood Holdings could have what they wanted—something real, not just smoke and mirrors—and then whispered that I never wanted it this way, the Ace of Spades still hidden in my hand.
I told him, 'You'll walk with me,' holding the Ace behind my back, feeling the edge press into my finger—right before I threw it.
I stepped hard and slung the Ace like a blade—it hit him square in the right eye, blood popping at the brow; he went down roaring.
I was digging at my chest, trying to shake the numbness, and all I could think was that I had to make the call to Carson Colter—before everything slipped away.

I was on the phone, clutching my chest, trying to breathe through the spasms when Carson Colter said they revoked the deal—I couldn’t get air, just kept gasping, 'They what? What? No. No. Why?' like it might change anything.

I turned and saw that thing—Casey Keller’s face torn apart, a the small case pointed at my head, and then Sage Hart standing there like this was all under control—I barely got out 'Doc-- y-- wha-- what is this?' before my pulse went wild.

I heard Avery Sinclair say it—'They're father and son'—and suddenly everything about my mother, Valerie Sawyer, the way he looked at me, it snapped into place. I'm his. I'm actually his goddamn blood.
I saw him looking at me through the tubes and wires, and I locked eyes with him—no words, just hate, raw and deep. I don't know if he felt it, but I meant every second of that glare.

memories.memory_text: I adjusted the record level on the console just as the V-U meters spiked and began to modulate, making sure we captured Owen Wilder's voice clearly.
I tweaked the frequency on the digital console and keyed the mic to command the camera team—'Zoom and pan please. Stay tight.'—keeping the feed locked on the figure moving inside the mansion.

I remember questioning whether Valerie Sawyer was really a double agent—something didn't add up about his loyalty, and the way Avery Sinclair paused before launching into that full history made me sure there was more beneath it.

I remember the photos flashing on the screen—Valerie Sawyer with Sinatra, Darian Wilder at the casino opening, then late-night meetings with Valerie Sawyer’s men—and realizing he wasn’t just rising through the ranks, he was orchestrating a takeover that split the entire family apart.

I asked if Wesley Hale could be involved in the Darian Wilder hit—his history fits the kind of brutality we're seeing, and the idea that someone like him might be loose on a million-dollar contract unsettled me.
I told them it was the last place they'd look—Darian Wilder has to be intercepted before Robin Thorne takes him back to Vegas, and I made sure they understood the weight of what's at stake.

I remember pulling off the headphones after hearing Owen Wilder mention Morgan Cavendish—some supposed hitman with a million-dollar rate, but Blair Ellison said there's no record of him. I wondered if that meant he was just made up, or if he was really that good—never caught, no trace.

I flipped through the photos of Reese Bellamy and Owen Wilder again, thinking about how they're risking everything by moving directly against Valerie Sawyer—going to Darian Wilder, setting up a high-stakes play. The odds are long, and it felt like desperation, not strategy.
I held up the file and counted thirty-six plastic surgeries—nose, eyes, chin, jaw redone over and over. I couldn't believe a man had been cut this much and we never knew.
I flipped to a photo paper-clipped in the file—Valerie Sawyer, murdered. I remember asking why Northstar Studios never moved on Valerie Sawyer for that, knowing he killed one of ours.

I remember demanding to know if the Justice lawyers had signed off before we moved, and when they hadn't, I still pushed to lock down the Riverside Hospital—Darian Wilder couldn't be allowed to flee, even without full clearance.

I heard the deputy describe a handwritten receipt for maroon uniforms found on Robin Thorne’s body—no rental company name, just the color listed. That detail stood out immediately; it was too specific to be random.

I was on the phone with the deputy when Blair Ellison told me he was going to Riverside Hospital. I said I’d take the car to the lake. We both plugged in our earpieces. I asked if he was going up to the Riverside Hospital alone—he pulled his .45 and checked the chamber. Then Rowan Cavendish’ voice came through.

I held the evidence bag with the severed fingers, still not fully grasping what I was looking at—frostbitten, shot off—and only then did it hit me: Cameron Davenport, a known associate of Robin Thorne, was now a victim.

When the Task Force Chief said they found Robin Thorne's rental car at Riverside Hospital parking structure, I immediately asked where it was now—my voice tightened, sensing the situation was already slipping beyond containment.
I arrived with the team, securing the parking structure and locking down access to the Riverside Hospital level—Eastwood Holdings already chaining the door shut behind us.

I saw the Taylor Sterling trembling, nails chewed raw, and when he said another agent had taken Blair Ellison—someone claiming to be from San Francisco with a Spanish name—I felt the air shift. The moment he said 'Garcia or Diego,' I knew it wasn't one of ours.

When the agent confirmed the man wasn't from our office, I didn't hesitate—I ordered them to run the names through the D.C. database, my voice sharp over the lobby noise. The fact that he wore security attire and moved freely changed everything; we were no longer in control.

I was in the Lakeview School, trying to filter through the static on my the weathered jacket, when a broken transmission came through—Rowan Cavendish saying there were two men, Gerald D and Blair Ellison, and questioning which one was real.
For just a split second, the signal cleared—and I heard Rowan Cavendish say, 'Cuz I'mma kill the one that ain't,' and I knew it wasn't a warning, it was a promise.
I positioned my team at the far end of the hallway, keeping the Lakeview School in sight—every move had to be silent, controlled, ready for what was coming.
I positioned the team in a two-man cover formation at the far end of the hallway, eyes on the open Lakeview School—possible hostiles inside, ready for fire.
I was pressing down on Blair Ellison' chest, again and again, trying to get his heart started—felt the bone give slightly under my hands, but nothing. He wasn't breathing.
I was pounding on Blair Ellison' chest, trying to bring him back, but he was gone—completely gone. I couldn't save him, and then I just broke, sobbing over his body.

Something slipped from my pocket—Cameron Davenport's bag of severed fingers—and I didn't even remember keeping them. Looking at Blair Ellison' hand, missing fingers too, I almost laughed at how insane it all was.
I was unaccounted for after the operation went down—Avery Sinclair had to order my location confirmed, and that phone call from Casey Keller’s device was the only trace of me.

I kicked open the stairwell door, adrenaline surging as I burst into the hallway—only to see Morgan Cavendish stepping out of the Lakeview School with Valerie Sawyer’s men, weapons drawn, at the exact same moment.

I pointed at Morgan Cavendish and demanded answers—'This is him? The hitman hired to kill Darian Wilder? He's a doctor?'—and Avery Sinclair just stood there, touching my arm like that made any of it okay.

Casey Keller jumped out the window—just launched himself—and for a second he was suspended in the air, like some twisted piece of art against the sky, then he was gone. And nobody reacted. Nobody cared.
I pulled the plastic bag with the severed fingers from my pocket and held it out to Cameron Davenport, watching his face as he recognized what was inside.
After seeing his bandaged hand and hearing him say he just wanted to go home, I offered to drive him—Las Vegas was his home, but he didn’t make it easy to help.
I walked in clean, suit pressed, no tie, and flashed a badge that wasn't mine—just nodded when the orderly asked if I was with the third-floor group. One silent confirmation and I was through.
I pressed the the small case into Avery Sinclair's side and made him walk with me—he looked stunned, pale, like he couldn't believe I'd do it, but I needed answers now, not later.
I demanded to know why no one called us about Darian Wilder's situation being altered, why my partner's body was already being prepared for cremation while they covered up the truth.
I remembered the paternity suit from 1967—filed against Valerie Sawyer by Noel Langley, Darian Wilder’s mother. It clicked the moment Avery Sinclair said they were father and son.
Avery Sinclair started to say they figured out who Valerie Sawyer actually was—then stopped himself. I saw him realize he’d said too much.
